section.title: A Prayer for Restoration
section.sectionRationale: The book ends not with a dirge but with a prayer. The fifth poem drops the acrostic form, as if grief has finally become direct address, and the whole community turns as one to plead with God. They lay out their disgrace, confess their sin, and rest everything on the one unshaken fact left to them: You, O LORD, reign forever. It closes with the book's boldest request and its most honest fear, holding both together before the throne.
section.thesis: Stripped of everything, the community turns from lament to direct prayer, spreading their disgrace before the eternal King, confessing that they have sinned, and casting themselves on the God who reigns forever with the plea, Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, so we may return.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the community spreads its disgrace before God, 5:1 to 18; the anchor of hope, You, O LORD, reign forever, 5:19; and the closing plea and honest fear, Restore us to Yourself, unless You have utterly rejected us, 5:20 to 22.

units.label: Remember, O LORD, our disgrace
units.note: the community spreads out its suffering

verses.text: {{zakar|Remember}}, O LORD, what has happened to us. Look and see our disgrace!
Our {{nachalah|inheritance}} has been turned over to strangers, our houses to foreigners.
We have become fatherless orphans; our mothers are widows.
We must buy the water we drink; our wood comes at a price.
We are closely pursued; we are weary and find no rest.
We submitted to Egypt and Assyria to get enough bread.
Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we bear their punishment.
Slaves rule over us; there is no one to deliver us from their hands.
We get our bread at the risk of our lives because of the sword in the wilderness.
Our skin is as hot as an oven with fever from our hunger.
Women have been ravished in Zion, virgins in the cities of Judah.
Princes have been hung up by their hands; elders receive no respect.
Young men toil at millstones; boys stagger under loads of wood.
The elders have left the city gate; the young men have stopped their music.
Joy has left our hearts; our dancing has turned to mourning.
The crown has fallen from our head. Woe to us, for we have sinned!
Because of this, our hearts are faint; because of these, our eyes grow dim,
because of Mount Zion, which lies desolate, patrolled by foxes.
You, O LORD, reign forever; Your throne endures from generation to generation.

units.label: Restore us to Yourself
units.note: the closing plea and honest fear

verses.text: Why have You forgotten us forever? Why have You forsaken us for so long?
{{shuv|Restore}} us to Yourself, O LORD, so we may return; renew our days as of old,
unless You have utterly rejected us and remain angry with us beyond measure.

zakar.gloss: To remember, and in Scripture to remember is to act, not merely to recall. When Israel asks the LORD to remember, they are pleading with Him to step in and do something about their plight, as He remembered His covenant and rescued them from Egypt.

nachalah.gloss: Inheritance, the land the LORD gave each family as their permanent portion, a sign of belonging in the promised land. To have the inheritance handed to strangers is to lose the tangible pledge of the covenant, which makes the loss far deeper than mere property.

shuv.gloss: To turn, return, restore. The same root carries both halves of the plea: restore us and we will return. It is the word for repentance, turning back to God, and here the people confess that even their turning must be God's gift, restore us that we may return.

basic.context: The last chapter is a prayer, and everyone prays it together. Notice the words us and we all the way through: this is the whole community on its knees. They stop describing the ruin from a distance and simply spread it out before God, orphans and widows, paying for their own water, ruled by slaves, joy gone, the crown fallen. They confess it plainly, woe to us, for we have sinned. Then, in one bright verse, they lay hold of the only thing that has not been shaken: You, O LORD, reign forever. On that ground they make the book's boldest request, Restore us to Yourself, so we may return, and end with an honest, trembling fear that God might have rejected them for good.
basic.hermeneutics: The dropping of the acrostic here is likely deliberate: the tidy alphabet gives way to raw, direct pleading. The center of gravity is verse 19, the one solid rock, God still reigns, His throne outlasts every empire that has fallen on them. Everything else in the prayer leans on that. The key move is in verse 21: they do not say we will pull ourselves together; they ask God to restore them so that they can return. Even repentance is understood as a gift only God can give. And the book ends unresolved, on a plea, which teaches us that faith can live in the tension of waiting.
basic.originalLanguages: The prayer opens with zakar, remember, and in the Bible when God remembers He acts; they are begging Him to intervene, as He once remembered His covenant and saved them from Egypt. Their nachalah, their inheritance, the family land that pledged their place in the covenant, is now in strangers' hands, a loss far deeper than property. And the closing plea turns on shuv, to return or restore: restore us that we may return, confessing that even their turning back to God must be His work.
basic.typology: The community that cannot restore itself and must cry restore us to Yourself pictures the human condition that only God can heal, fulfilled when God draws sinners to Himself through Christ. The eternal throne that endures forever is the throne of the LORD, established in the risen and reigning Christ. And the honest fear of being rejected forever is answered by the Son who was rejected and forsaken in our place so that we never would be.
basic.christ: The prayer restore us to Yourself, so we may return finds its answer in Jesus, through whom God turns sinners back to Himself. The eternal throne of verse 19 is the very throne now occupied by the risen Christ, whose kingdom will never end. And the book's most fearful line, that God might have utterly rejected them, is met at the cross, where Jesus is truly forsaken, why have You forsaken Me, absorbing the rejection our sin deserved so that God can say to us, I will never leave you nor forsake you.
basic.god: God is the eternal King whose throne outlasts every catastrophe: empires rise and fall, Jerusalem lies in ruins, but He reigns forever. He is the God who remembers and acts, the only one who can restore what is broken. And He is a God who welcomes brutally honest prayer, He receives both the bold request and the trembling fear, and does not turn away the ones who come pleading.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 80 repeats the plea restore us, O God, that we may be saved. Psalm 102 celebrates the LORD enthroned forever while Zion lies in ruins. Jeremiah 31 promises the new covenant and return. Matthew 27 records Jesus forsaken in our place, and Hebrews 13 promises He will never leave nor forsake His own.
basic.oneStory: The book of grief ends on its knees, resting everything on the God who reigns forever and pleading, restore us to Yourself. That prayer is the cry of every exile and every sinner, and God answers it in Christ, who is forsaken so we are welcomed home, and who reigns on the eternal throne, so that the days of God's people can truly be renewed.

context.literary:
Chapter 5 has twenty two verses, the length of the Hebrew alphabet, but it is no acrostic. The four earlier poems arranged their grief by letter; this one gives up the frame. Many readers hear in that a lowering of the formal guard: the poet has stopped composing and begun to pray. The lines are short and plain, and the whole is spoken in the first person plural. Not one 'I' stands in it. After the individual voices of chapters 1 to 3, the community speaks for itself.

The structure is a simple arc. Verse 1 is a cry in three commands, 'remember', 'look', 'see'. Verses 2 to 18 are a long inventory of loss, ordered by sphere of life: property in verse 2, family in verse 3, basic supplies in verse 4, political freedom in verses 5 to 9, the body and the women in verses 10 and 11, rank and labour in verses 12 to 13, and joy in verses 14 to 15. Verse 16 breaks the pattern with a plain, unqualified confession, 'Woe to us, for we have sinned', and verses 17 and 18 give the reason for the faint heart in a three-fold 'because of this, because of these, because of Mount Zion'.

Verse 19 stands alone, and the Hebrew sentence opens on the pronoun 'You', placed first for emphasis. It answers the crown that has fallen in verse 16 with a throne that has not. Verses 20 to 22 are the petition, and two echoes frame the chapter: the 'turned over' of verse 2 and the 'turned' of verse 15 are the same verb, and 'restore' and 'return' in verse 21 are one root. The book's last word in Hebrew is 'exceedingly', the same word that closes 'very good' in Genesis 1:31, now describing anger.
context.historical:
The poem is set after the fall, and it speaks for those who were left living under occupation. Their land has passed to strangers, verse 2, and the water and firewood they once gathered freely now cost money, verse 4. That fits the conditions of a conquered province, where the occupying power taxed and controlled the basics of life. Verse 8 complains that 'slaves rule over us', which may point to the lowest officials of the conquerors, or to the local men who profited under them. Nehemiah 9:36-37 voices the same sense of bondage a century later, with the harvest going to foreign kings.

Verse 6 looks back at a long national habit. Israel and Judah had often 'given the hand' to Egypt and Assyria to get bread and protection, as Hosea 12:1 says of Ephraim, who made a covenant with Assyria and sent olive oil to Egypt. Isaiah 30:1-3 had warned that the shade of Egypt would turn to shame. By Jerusalem's fall Assyria no longer existed as an empire, so the line likely recalls the whole record of reliance on foreign powers, not only the current policy.

Verse 7 grieves that 'our fathers sinned and are no more'. The prophets did trace the exile back to the reign of Manasseh, 2 Kings 21:10-16 and 2 Kings 23:26-27, and Jeremiah 15:4 says so in as many words. Verses 11 to 14 describe the cruelties of a defeated city: the abuse of women, the humiliation of princes, forced labour at the grindstone, and the silence of the city gate, where the elders once sat as judges. After the fall, Gedaliah was appointed governor and then murdered, 2 Kings 25:22-26, and many fled to Egypt, Jeremiah 43:5-7, so the survivors could not count on peace even in the wreckage.
context.canonical:
The chapter is a communal lament, and the Psalter is full of its relatives. Psalm 74 begins with the same 'Why have You rejected us forever?' and the same 'Remember', and its last line pleads for God not to forget. Psalm 79 and Psalm 80 add the refrain 'Restore us, O God', Psalm 80:3. The petition of Lamentations 5:21 also reappears nearly word for word in Jeremiah 31:18, where Ephraim prays, 'Restore me, that I may return, for You are the LORD my God', and in the very next verses God answers with a tender 'My heart yearns for him', Jeremiah 31:20. That answer is the shape of the canon's reply to this chapter.

The post exilic prayers pick up its words. Ezra 9:7-9 and Nehemiah 9:36-37 confess the same sin and the same slavery, and Daniel 9:16-19 prays for the city 'that bears Your name', pleading on God's compassion and not on the people's righteousness. Isaiah 63:15 to 64:12 is the nearest relative of all, where the people ask God to look down from heaven, call Him their Father, and say they are the clay in His hand, Isaiah 64:8.

The answer comes in the promises of a new heart, Ezekiel 36:26-28, and a new covenant, Jeremiah 31:33-34. In the New Testament the prayer 'renew our days' is taken up in the language of newness: the Spirit renews the inner self daily, 2 Corinthians 4:16, and the One on the throne says, 'Behold, I make all things new', Revelation 21:5. The cry of Lamentations 5:20 is picked up by Jesus on the cross, Matthew 27:46, using the same verb of forsaking as Psalm 22:1, and the assurance of Hebrews 13:5 is its reply.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet wants his community to learn a way of praying, not just to feel a sorrow. The people could have gone on telling their story to one another or to the nations. Instead, the poem turns them to face God and say everything. It insists that the proper place to bring a ruined inheritance, a fatherless home and a hunger that burns like fever is the presence of the One who allowed it, because He alone can change it.

He also intends the confession to be shared and personal at once. Verse 7 admits that the weight of earlier generations is real, and verse 16 will not let the present generation hide behind it. The poet wants the people to carry both truths without turning either into an excuse. The first would make them victims; the second keeps them honest.

The pivot of verse 19 is meant to retune everything else. After eighteen verses of what has changed, the poet says what has not. The first readers were being taught that circumstances could not be the measure of God, and that His throne was a larger fact than their ruin. The closing lines show that this confidence does not remove the pain of waiting, and the poet does not pretend that it does. He wants people who can hold an unshaken doctrine and an unanswered question in the same breath.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the chapter is description, and some of it is hard to apply directly. The unjust conditions it lists, slavery, abuse, forced labour and public humiliation, are what happened to a conquered people. The poem does not call any of it good, and it does not command anyone to accept injustice. Its remedy is not passive. The people call out to God, who in Scripture is the defender of widows and orphans, Psalm 68:5, and the poem leaves room for every legitimate effort to relieve suffering.

What is prescriptive is the pattern of prayer: tell God exactly what has happened, own what is yours to own, and rest on His rule before asking for anything. Verse 19 is placed ahead of the petition so that the request grows out of the doctrine. It is the same order Jesus gave when He taught His disciples to pray, with the Father's name and kingdom before the daily bread.

The poem also models how to ask for repentance. Believers are not told to resolve to do better and then to come back. They are shown a prayer that asks God to bring them back. That can be read next to Jeremiah 31:18 and Acts 5:31, and it keeps repentance from becoming a human achievement.

debates.question: How should we read the final verse, 'unless You have utterly rejected us'?

views.label: A fear that stays inside the prayer
views.case: The Hebrew opens with a phrase that can mean 'unless' or 'for rather'. If it is 'unless', the poet voices a real possibility and leaves it with God, so the book ends on honest uncertainty that nevertheless sits inside a prayer. The prayer itself is evidence that the poet expects an answer.

views.label: A bitter statement of what seems to be true
views.case: Others take the clause as a flat assertion, 'for You have utterly rejected us', so that the book closes on an unresolved sense of rejection. The ending then echoes laments like Psalm 88 that stop in the dark, and it tells the reader that faith is not always granted a bright last line.

views.label: A deliberately open ending that the canon completes
views.case: Jewish practice at the public reading of this book was to repeat verse 21 after verse 22, so that the congregation does not finish on the harsh note. That custom reflects a reading in which the book's silence waits for later Scripture to speak, as Jeremiah 31:20 and Isaiah 54:7-8 do.

debates.bearing: The grammar allows more than one reading, and the poet may intend the ambiguity. What is clear is that the poem does not let the fear have the last word in the heart, because the petition of verse 21 is already addressed to the God who might refuse it.

debates.question: How do verse 7 and verse 16 fit together?

views.label: Inherited consequences are real
views.case: The prophets did link the exile with sins long before, 2 Kings 21:10-16 and Jeremiah 15:4. The covenant language of Exodus 34:7 speaks of visiting the iniquity of the fathers on later generations, so the poem is reading its own situation in that light.

views.label: Each generation answers for its own sin
views.case: Ezekiel 18:2-20 and Jeremiah 31:29-30 reject the proverb about fathers eating sour grapes, and Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids punishing children for their fathers' crimes. On that view verse 7 is a sufferer's partial perception, and verse 16 supplies the full truth: 'we have sinned'.

debates.bearing: The prayer holds both. A generation can feel the weight of a history it did not write while owning the share it did, and the poem models that honesty in the same breath, without letting either side cancel the other.

debates.question: Who are the 'slaves' who rule in verse 8?

views.label: Low ranking foreign officials
views.case: The word may describe functionaries of the conquering power who now hold authority over former nobles, a reversal that shames the princes of verse 12.

views.label: Local people raised above their station
views.case: Others see subordinate men who took power under the occupation, in line with the reversal of Proverbs 30:21-22, where a servant who becomes king makes the earth tremble.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle the identity, and the point lies in the inversion itself: a covenant people made to serve those who should have served them, with no one to deliver them.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 gives three imperatives, zekhor, 'remember', habbita, 'look', and re'eh, 'see'. The second verb, from nabat, is to look closely and steadily, and the third is the ordinary word for seeing. The poet is stacking them to bring God's attention down from a distance onto one spot. The word that follows, cherpah, is disgrace or reproach, the shame that sticks to a people mocked by its neighbours, as in Psalm 79:4.

In verse 2 the 'inheritance' is nachalah, the family plot received by lot and meant to stay in the family, Leviticus 25:23. Naboth refused to sell his for exactly that reason, 1 Kings 21:3. Losing it cut a household out of the covenant's physical form. The same verse says the inheritance 'has been turned over', from haphak, and verse 15 uses the same verb of dancing 'turned to mourning'. One root joins the loss of the land and the loss of the joy.

Verse 3 calls the people 'fatherless', yetomim, and their mothers 'widows', almanot. In the law these two are God's special wards, Exodus 22:22-24, and Psalm 68:5 calls Him 'a father of the fatherless'. The people have become the very kind of people the LORD promised to guard, and they say so in the hope He will recognise them.

Verse 4 sets the ordinary word for silver, kesef, beside the drinking of water, so that they drink 'for silver'. The people pay for what was free. Verse 6 'we submitted' is literally 'we gave the hand', an idiom of submission, and the stated aim, 'to get enough bread', puts a cheap price on a people's loyalty.

Verse 16 is the confession, chatanu, 'we have sinned', one of the most basic words for sin, meaning to miss the mark. It is given in the plural and in the perfect tense, an owned and finished act. Verses 17 and 18 begin three times with al, 'because of', the repetition tying the fainting heart to the ruin of Mount Zion. The word for the 'foxes' there is shu'al, which covers jackals as well, Psalm 63:10. The animals that now walk on the holy hill are a sign of an abandoned place.

In verse 19 the verb for 'reign' is yashab, 'sit', and the line is nearly identical to Psalm 102:12 in Hebrew. The pronoun 'You' leads the sentence. The verb for 'forgotten' in verse 20 is shakach, and 'forsaken' is azav. The second is the verb in Psalm 22:1, which Jesus quotes on the cross, Matthew 27:46.

Verse 21 pairs two forms of one root, hashivenu, 'cause us to return', in the causative stem, and nashuvah, 'that we may return', in the simple stem. God does the turning, and the people turn. The same pairing appears in Jeremiah 31:18. The petition 'renew' is chadesh, from the word for new, which Psalm 51:10 uses in 'renew a right spirit', and 'of old' translates qedem, the earlier days of the covenant.

typology.fulfillment: The land was Israel's tangible share in the promise, and its loss in the exile is the family's loss of a place in God's plan. The correspondence is with the believer's inheritance, which Peter says is 'imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you', 1 Peter 1:4. The escalation is that the New Testament's inheritance cannot be taken, sold, or conquered, and Paul says it is guaranteed by the Spirit, Ephesians 1:13-14. The type falls short in its materiality: the land could be lost, while the inheritance of Christ's people is held by the Son, who has Himself been given the nations, Psalm 2:8.

Israel in ruins describes itself as orphaned, and the promise that answers it comes from Jesus on the night before He is taken: 'I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you', John 14:18. Paul says believers received a spirit of adoption by which they cry 'Abba, Father', Romans 8:15. The escalation is from being protected by the Father of the fatherless to being made His children in the Son. The type falls short because Israel's orphanhood was a consequence of sin, whereas believers are brought into the family by a grace they did not earn, and the Father of Luke 15:20 runs to meet the wayward child.

The throne of the LORD outlasts every fallen crown, and in the New Testament that throne is occupied by the risen Son. Hebrews 1:8 applies the words 'Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever' to Him, and the angel promises Mary that He will receive the throne of David and reign forever, Luke 1:32-33. The correspondence is the permanence of the throne, and the escalation is that the king on it is now a man who has died and risen. Because He reigns, believers 'approach the throne of grace with confidence', Hebrews 4:16. The type cannot reach as far as the Lamb in the middle of the throne, Revelation 5:6, because Lamentations does not yet know a king who reigns by being slain.

The plea that God Himself would turn His people back finds its fulfilment in the work of the exalted Christ, whom God 'exalted to His right hand as Prince and Savior, in order to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel', Acts 5:31. The prayer asked for something only God could do, and the gospel says He did it by giving His Son and His Spirit, Ezekiel 36:26-27. The renewal that the poet asks 'as of old' is surpassed, for it is not a return to the former days but a new creation, 2 Corinthians 5:17 and Revelation 21:5. The type falls short because the restoration of the Babylonian return left the heart unchanged, as the prophets later complain.

study.christ:
The prayer leads to Christ first through the figure of the throne. Verse 19 puts a throne beside a ruin, and it was always going to be asked whose throne remains when the Davidic one has fallen. The Gospels answer that the angel announces to Mary a son who will have David's throne and a kingdom with no end, Luke 1:32-33, and Hebrews 1:8 applies the verse of Psalm 45 about a throne that endures forever and ever to the Son. The poet's confidence that God sits forever is vindicated in a particular Person, and the New Testament does not tie the throne to a building or a bloodline but to the risen Lord, Revelation 11:15.

It leads to Christ in the plea for restoration. Verse 21 asks God to do the returning in His people, which the covenant pictures as the heart of the new covenant, Jeremiah 31:33-34 and Ezekiel 36:26-28. Peter preaches that God has exalted Jesus 'to grant repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel', Acts 5:31, so that turning back is itself a gift flowing from the cross and the empty tomb. Jesus's parable of the father who runs down the road to the returning son, Luke 15:20, is the shape of the answer: while the sinner is 'still in the distance' the Father moves first.

It leads to Christ by way of the words 'Why have You forgotten us forever? Why have You forsaken us?' The Hebrew verb for forsaking, azav, is the verb in Psalm 22:1, and Jesus takes that psalm onto His lips on the cross, Matthew 27:46. The people feared that they might be utterly rejected. The Gospels show the One who was not rejected as a sinner meeting that very rejection so that those who come to Him are not, Hebrews 13:5 and Romans 8:38-39. Isaiah 49:14-16 had already answered the cry of a forsaken Zion with the promise that God would not forget, as a mother could not forget her nursing child.

It leads to Christ in the way the book is left unfinished. The ending of Lamentations is not an answer but a posture of waiting, and the New Testament's tone of 'already and not yet' belongs to the same stance. The Lord who wept over Jerusalem and whose heart longed to gather her children, Matthew 23:37-39, is the One who brings the lamenters home.

The reading must stay honest. The prayer is Israel's, and its first answer was in history: a return, a rebuilt temple, a people preserved. We do not need to make every verse a coded sentence about Jesus. The link rests on the way the New Testament itself takes up the throne, the plea for restoration and the cry of forsakenness, and on the way the book's unanswered question finds a place to be answered.
study.god:
The pivot of the chapter is a statement about God, and it shapes all the rest. Verse 19 does not claim that God has been good lately, or that the evidence supports Him. It states what He is: He sits as king forever, and His throne is a thing that goes from generation to generation. That claim sits between a catalogue of ruin on one side and a petition on the other, so it can be read as the reason the petition is not mad. This God does not rise and fall with His people's fortunes, and His kingship is not dependent on the standing of a temple. The surrounding poem puts a fallen crown in verse 16 next to this enduring throne, and the contrast is the doctrine.

He is a God who can be addressed with everything. The poem lists hunger, fever, forced labour, shame, and the grief of old men who no longer sit in the gate, and it addresses all of it to Him. Psalms such as 44:23-24 and 89:46 push even harder, asking why He sleeps and how long He will hide. The fact that Scripture preserves such prayers tells us that God does not require His people to edit their grief before they bring it, and that bold complaint is not unbelief when it is addressed to Him.

He is the God who remembers. The opening plea, 'Remember', draws on a pattern in the Bible where God's remembering is the start of His action. In Exodus 2:24 God heard their groaning and remembered His covenant, and the exodus followed. The poet is asking God to do again what He has done before, and so grounds the prayer in His own recorded character, Exodus 34:6-7, rather than in the people's merit.

He is holy and merciful together. The confession in verse 16 never questions that the judgment was deserved. Yet the petition reaches for the compassion of the same character: 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion'. The earlier chapter had said His mercies are new every morning, Lamentations 3:22-23, and that He does not cast off forever, 3:31-33. Chapter 5 asks Him to be that God now.

He is the one who restores. The verb in verse 21 puts the initiative where it belongs, and it quietly confesses that the people cannot repair themselves. For worship, this means praise can be spoken in the dark and that confidence rests on who God is, not on how things look. The last verse's fear is not a lapse in worship but part of it, since it is brought to God rather than held away from Him.

crossReferences.note: Almost the same Hebrew sentence as verse 19: the LORD sits enthroned forever while Zion lies in need of compassion. The psalm goes on to say the time has come to favour Zion, which supplies the answer Lamentations 5 is still waiting for.

Another communal lament that starts with 'Why have You rejected us forever?' and asks God to remember His congregation and Mount Zion. The two texts share the vocabulary of rejection, remembering and the desolate holy hill, so the poet is praying in an inherited language.

The refrain 'Restore us, O God, and cause Your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved' is the same plea as verse 21. The psalm adds that salvation consists in the shining of God's face, so restoration is relational before it is political.

Ephraim prays, 'Restore me, that I may return', using the same causative and simple forms of one verb as verse 21. The very next lines have God answer with compassion: 'My heart yearns for him.' It is the fullest biblical reply to the prayer of Lamentations 5.

A prayer from the ruins that asks God to look down from heaven, call Him Father, and wonders why He has let the people stray. It shares the voice and the longing of Lamentations 5, and it is followed by the great plea 'that You would rend the heavens and come down'.

'You are our Father; we are the clay.' The people ask not to be remembered in iniquity forever, as they ask in Lamentations 5:20 and 22 not to be forgotten forever. It shows the same combination of confession and appeal to God's fatherly mercy.

God heard the groaning and remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. The verb 'remember' in Lamentations 5:1 asks for the same action: for God to act on His promises, not merely to recall them.

Daniel prays for the desolate city that bears God's name, with confession of sin and a plea based on compassion, not merit. Its closing words, 'do not delay', answer the sense of long silence in Lamentations 5:20.

God's answer to the proverb about fathers eating sour grapes. It guards against reading Lamentations 5:7 as an excuse, because each person answers for his own sin, which is why verse 16 says 'we have sinned'.

Jesus cries 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' using the verb of forsaking that appears in Lamentations 5:20. The Gospels show Him entering the abandonment that the lament fears, so that His people are not finally abandoned.

'Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.' The promise is the direct reverse of the fear in Lamentations 5:20 and 22, and it is applied to every believer because Christ has already borne the forsaking.

God dwells with His people, wipes away every tear, and says 'I make all things new'. The prayer 'renew our days' receives its final answer, and the exiled joy of Lamentations 5:15 returns as the end of mourning.

study.oneStory:
The prayer stands at one of the lowest points of the biblical story, and its fear is the oldest in the book. In Genesis the first sin ended with a man and woman driven out and the way back guarded, and every sentence of exile since has been a version of that expulsion. The poem is the exile of a nation, and it carries the same question: can those sent away be brought home? The covenant itself had said they could. Deuteronomy 30:1-3 says that when the people call the curses and the blessings to mind in the lands where they are scattered and return to the LORD, He will restore them from captivity and have compassion. Lamentations 5 is the prayer of people trying to do that.

The poem also sets up what comes next. The postexilic prayers of Ezra, Nehemiah and Daniel take up its confession, and the return under Cyrus gives a partial answer, though Ezra 9:9 can still say they are slaves. The prophets look further, to a heart that God Himself changes, Ezekiel 36:26-28, and to a covenant in which sins are forgiven and remembered no more, Jeremiah 31:33-34. Those promises are what the question 'Have You utterly rejected us?' is waiting for.

The answer arrives in Jesus. He is the king whose throne does not fall, Luke 1:32-33. He is the one forsaken so that the forsaken might be gathered, Matthew 27:46, and the one who grants the repentance that the poem begged God to give, Acts 5:31. He lets the exiles know that they will not be left as orphans, John 14:18. His Spirit makes the inner self new day by day, 2 Corinthians 4:16, and the final days are not those of old but something larger.

At the end of the story the throne of verse 19 stands at the centre of a city where there is no longer any curse and where God's servants see His face, Revelation 22:3-4. The fox-haunted hill is replaced by the new Jerusalem, the fatherless are welcomed to the Father's house, and the God who sat enthroned through the ruin dwells with His people for good, Revelation 21:3. The long prayer of Lamentations 5 is not wasted, because every part of it is answered there.

quiz.q: What is distinctive about the form and voice of Lamentations 5?

options.text: It drops the acrostic form and is prayed by the whole community together in the first person plural, us and we.
options.note: Ordered lament gives way to direct, communal prayer.

options.text: It is a prayer spoken by the gathered people rather than a lone voice.
options.note: True, and it also notably abandons the acrostic structure of the earlier poems.

options.text: It is a song of triumph celebrating Zion's rebuilding.
options.note: It laments ongoing disgrace and pleads for restoration; the rebuilding has not come.

options.text: It is a list of laws for the returning exiles.
options.note: It is a communal prayer, not legal instruction.

quiz.q: What is the one unshaken anchor of the prayer, in verse 19?

options.text: That the LORD reigns forever and His throne endures from generation to generation.
options.note: God's eternal reign is the solid ground on which the whole prayer rests.

options.text: That God is still on His throne despite the ruin.
options.note: True, and specifically His throne outlasts every empire and generation.

options.text: That the walls of Jerusalem were still standing.
options.note: The city lies desolate; the anchor is God's reign, not the city's condition.

options.text: That their enemies had finally repented.
options.note: The prayer rests on God's eternal kingship, not on the enemies.

quiz.q: What does the plea Restore us to Yourself, so we may return, teach about repentance?

options.text: That even turning back to God is His gift; they ask God to restore them so that they are able to return.
options.note: The one root shuv carries both God's restoring and their returning.

options.text: That they needed God's help to come back to Him.
options.note: True, and precisely that their very repentance depends on God restoring them first.

options.text: That they could restore themselves by trying harder.
options.note: The prayer asks God to do the restoring; it does not rely on their own effort.

options.text: That returning to God was no longer possible.
options.note: They earnestly ask to return; the plea assumes it is possible by God's grace.

quiz.q: How does the community handle its guilt in this prayer?

options.text: It both feels the weight of its fathers' sin and personally confesses, woe to us, for we have sinned.
options.note: Inherited consequence and personal responsibility are held together, 5:7 and 5:16.

options.text: It owns its own sin while acknowledging a shared history of sin.
options.note: True, and it refuses to hide behind the ancestors, taking personal responsibility.

options.text: It blames the previous generations entirely and claims innocence.
options.note: It says we have sinned; it does not claim innocence.

options.text: It denies that anyone had sinned at all.
options.note: It plainly confesses sin as the cause of their woe.

quiz.q: How does the book's fearful ending, unless You have utterly rejected us, point to Christ?

options.text: The fear of being forsaken forever is answered at the cross, where Christ is forsaken in our place so His people are never finally rejected.
options.note: Jesus bears the forsakenness so God can promise never to forsake His own.

options.text: It shows a people who still hope even while fearing rejection.
options.note: True, and the gospel answers that fear in the forsaken and risen Christ.

options.text: It proves God had in fact rejected His people permanently.
options.note: The plea itself hopes otherwise, and Christ secures that they are not rejected.

options.text: It has no relation to Christ.
options.note: Christ's cry of forsakenness directly answers this fear.

questions: This whole chapter is prayed as we, not I. What difference might it make to bring your community's or family's troubles to God together, rather than always praying alone?
The people simply spread their disgrace out before God, holding nothing back. Is there something you have been too ashamed to name in prayer? What would it be like to lay it plainly before Him?
Everything in the prayer leans on verse 19, You, O LORD, reign forever. When your circumstances are shaking, how does the truth that God is still on the throne steady you?
They ask God to restore them so that they can return, treating even repentance as His gift. Where do you need to stop trying to fix yourself and ask God to do the turning in you?

The book ends on a plea, not a resolution, with the fear of being forsaken answered only later in Christ. How does it help to know you can pray honestly in the dark, trusting a God who was forsaken so that you never will be?

translationNotes.note: Remember translates zakar; in Scripture God's remembering is active, an appeal for Him to intervene, not merely to call something to mind.
Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we bear their punishment expresses the shared, inherited consequences of sin, held alongside the personal confession of 5:16.
Restore us so we may return uses one Hebrew root, shuv, for both God's restoring and the people's returning, quietly confessing that repentance itself is God's gift.
